stimuli.title: A Pond Food Web
stimuli.html:
The list below describes the feeding relationships in a small pond. Each arrow means "is eaten by."

  • Algae → zooplankton
  • Algae → snails
  • Zooplankton → minnows
  • Snails → crayfish
  • Minnows → bass
  • Crayfish → bass
  • Minnows → herons
  • Bass → herons

Ecologists estimate that only about 10% of the energy stored at one feeding level is passed on to the next level. The rest is used for life processes or lost as heat.

stimuli.title: Testing Conservation of Mass
stimuli.html:
Baking soda and vinegar react to produce carbon dioxide gas, water, and a dissolved salt. A student ran this reaction two ways.

Trial 1: She placed vinegar in an open flask, set a small cup of baking soda on the balance beside it, and recorded the total mass. She then poured the baking soda into the flask. Bubbles formed. When the bubbling stopped, she weighed the flask and empty cup again.

Trial 2: She repeated the same steps, but this time she used a plastic bottle. She lowered the small cup of baking soda into the bottle so that it rested above the vinegar without touching it, screwed the cap on tightly, and recorded the total mass. She then tipped the bottle to mix the substances. When the bubbling stopped, she weighed the sealed bottle again.

stimuli.title: Bacteria and Antibiotic Resistance
stimuli.html:
Bacteria reproduce quickly; under good conditions, some kinds divide every 20 minutes. In any large population of bacteria, a few cells may carry a random genetic mutation that lets them survive a particular antibiotic. When a patient takes that antibiotic, most of the bacteria die, but the resistant cells survive. The survivors then reproduce, passing the resistance gene to their offspring.

In a laboratory study, researchers grew a population of bacteria and exposed it to an antibiotic. After each round of exposure, they let the survivors regrow and then measured what percent of the population was resistant.

Round of exposure0 (start)1234
Resistant bacteria (%)18357296

Doctors warn that stopping an antibiotic too early, or using antibiotics when they are not needed, can speed up this process. When a course is stopped early, the bacteria that are hardest to kill are the ones most likely to be left alive. Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they have no effect on viruses, such as the viruses that cause the common cold.

stimuli.title: Keeping Blood Sugar in Balance
stimuli.html:
The human body keeps the level of glucose (sugar) in the blood within a narrow range. After a meal, glucose from digested food enters the blood, and the blood glucose level rises. The pancreas responds by releasing the hormone insulin. Insulin signals body cells, especially muscle and liver cells, to take in glucose from the blood, and the blood glucose level falls back toward normal.

Between meals, the blood glucose level slowly drops. The pancreas then releases a different hormone, glucagon, which signals the liver to release stored glucose into the blood. The blood glucose level rises back toward normal.

In type 1 diabetes, the pancreas makes little or no insulin, so a person with this condition must take insulin to keep blood glucose under control.

stimuli.title: Plate Boundaries
stimuli.html:
Earth's rigid outer layer, the lithosphere, is broken into large plates that move a few centimeters per year. Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur near the boundaries where plates meet.

At a divergent boundary, plates move apart. Magma rises to fill the gap, cools, and forms new crust. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge, an underwater mountain chain running down the middle of the Atlantic Ocean, is a divergent boundary. Over time, newly formed crust is carried away from the ridge on both sides as more new crust forms behind it.

At a convergent boundary, plates move toward each other. When a dense oceanic plate meets a less dense continental plate, the oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate in a process called subduction. Subduction forms a deep ocean trench offshore. As the plate sinks deep into the mantle, rock above it partly melts, and the magma rises to build a chain of volcanoes on the continent.

At a transform boundary, plates slide past each other horizontally. Crust is neither created nor destroyed, but stress builds up along the boundary and is released as earthquakes.

items.prompt: In this experiment, what is the independent variable?
options: The distance between the lamp and the test tube
The number of bubbles released per minute
The temperature of the water
The amount of baking soda in the water
items.explain:
The independent variable is the factor the experimenter deliberately changes. The student moved the lamp to 10, 20, 30, and 40 cm, so the distance from the lamp is the independent variable.

The number of bubbles is the dependent variable, because it is what she measured in response. Water temperature was held at 22 °C, so it is a controlled variable, not the one being tested.
why: The bubble count is what the student measured in response, so it is the dependent variable. The independent variable is the one she changed on purpose: the lamp distance.
The passage says the water was kept at 22 °C in every trial, so temperature was held constant (a controlled variable). The variable she changed was the lamp distance.
The baking soda was added once to supply carbon dioxide; the passage never says its amount was changed. The variable the student changed from trial to trial was the lamp distance.

items.prompt: What is the mean number of bubbles per minute at a distance of 20 cm? Enter a whole number.
items.explain:
Mean = sum of trials ÷ number of trials.

31 + 27 + 29 = 87
87 ÷ 3 = 29

Divide by 3, the number of trials, not by 4 (the number of distances tested).

mistakes.why: You divided by 4 (the number of distances) instead of 3 (the number of trials). 87 ÷ 3 = 29.
87 is the sum of the three trials. The mean divides that sum by the number of trials: 87 ÷ 3 = 29.
You may have averaged the 10 cm and 30 cm means instead of using the 20 cm row. Use the 20 cm trials: (31 + 27 + 29) ÷ 3 = 29.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: The plant stops photosynthesizing when the lamp is more than 30 cm away.
The rate of photosynthesis decreases as the plant receives less light.
Water temperature is the main factor that controls the rate of photosynthesis.
The rate of photosynthesis increases as the lamp is moved farther away.
items.explain:
As the lamp moves farther away, less light reaches the plant, and the mean bubble count falls steadily: 40 → 29 → 19 → 10. Bubbles are a measure of the rate of photosynthesis, so the rate decreases as the plant receives less light.

The plant did not stop at 40 cm; it still released about 10 bubbles per minute. Temperature was held constant, so the experiment gives no evidence about temperature. The rate went down, not up, with distance.
why: The plant did not stop: at 40 cm it still released about 10 bubbles per minute. The data show the rate falling with less light, not reaching zero.
Temperature was held at 22 °C in every trial, so this experiment gives no evidence about temperature. Only the lamp distance changed.
You reversed the trend. The mean bubble count fell from 40 to 10 as the lamp moved farther away, so the rate decreased.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements about the experiment.

The gas in the bubbles is mostly {{0}}, which the plant releases as a product of photosynthesis. The student dissolved baking soda in the water so that the plant would have enough {{1}} to carry out photosynthesis.

options: oxygen
carbon dioxide
nitrogen
hydrogen
why: Carbon dioxide is taken in by the plant as a raw material; it is not the gas released. Photosynthesis gives off oxygen, which forms the bubbles.
Nitrogen is not a product of photosynthesis. The equation is carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, so the bubbles are oxygen.
Plants do not release hydrogen gas in photosynthesis. The gas given off is oxygen.

options: oxygen
glucose
carbon dioxide
nitrogen
why: Oxygen is a product the plant releases, not something it needs to be supplied with. The passage says the baking soda supplied carbon dioxide.
Glucose is what the plant makes, not something it takes in from the water. The baking soda supplied carbon dioxide, a reactant.
Nitrogen is not a reactant in photosynthesis. The passage states that baking soda was added to supply carbon dioxide.

items.explain:
Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide + water → (light energy) → glucose + oxygen. The oxygen produced escapes as bubbles from the stem.

The passage states that the baking soda was added to supply carbon dioxide, a raw material (reactant) of photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide is an input, not the gas being released, and glucose is a product the plant makes, not something it absorbs from the water.

items.prompt: What was the average speed of the toy car over the 8 seconds shown? Enter your answer as a decimal.
items.explain:
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.

6.0 m ÷ 8 s = 0.75 m/s

A common error is dividing time by distance (8 ÷ 6.0 ≈ 1.33), which gives seconds per meter, not meters per second.

mistakes.why: You divided time by distance (8 ÷ 6.0), which gives seconds per meter. Speed is distance ÷ time: 6.0 ÷ 8 = 0.75 m/s.
6.0 m is the total distance, not the speed. Divide by the 8 seconds: 6.0 ÷ 8 = 0.75 m/s.
You divided one 2-second gain (1.5 m) by the full 8 seconds. Use the total distance over the total time: 6.0 ÷ 8 = 0.75 m/s.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the car's motion during the 8 seconds?
options: It sped up, because its distance from the starting line kept increasing.
It moved at a constant speed, because it covered the same distance in each 2-second interval.
It slowed down, because the graph does not curve upward.
It stayed in one place, because the graph is a straight line.
items.explain:
In every 2-second interval, the car traveled 1.5 m (0 → 1.5 → 3.0 → 4.5 → 6.0). Equal distances in equal times mean constant speed, which shows as a straight, sloped line on a distance-time graph.

An increasing distance alone does not mean the car sped up; any moving object gets farther from the start. Speeding up would show as larger and larger distance gains in each interval (a curve bending upward). A car standing still would show a flat, horizontal line.
why: An increasing distance alone does not mean speeding up; any moving object gets farther from the start. The car gained the same 1.5 m every 2 seconds, so its speed was constant.
A straight distance-time line means constant speed, not slowing. Slowing down would show smaller distance gains each interval, but the gains were all 1.5 m.
A straight line that slopes upward means steady motion. Standing still would be a flat, horizontal line, but the distance rose from 0 to 6.0 m.

items.prompt: Complete the Punnett square. What percent of the offspring from this cross are expected to have vestigial wings?
items.explain:
Fill in the square by combining one allele from each parent:

Ww
WWWWw
wWwww

Only ww flies show the recessive vestigial trait. That is 1 of 4 boxes: 1 ÷ 4 = 0.25 = 25%.

A common error is answering 50% by counting the two Ww boxes. Ww flies carry the vestigial allele but have normal wings, because W is dominant.

mistakes.why: You counted the two Ww boxes. Ww flies carry the vestigial allele but have normal wings because W is dominant. Only ww (1 of 4 boxes) is vestigial: 25%.
75% is the share with normal wings (WW, Ww, Ww). The question asks for vestigial wings, which only ww flies have: 1 of 4, or 25%.
0.25 is the fraction, but the question asks for a percent. Multiply by 100: 25%.

items.prompt: The researcher next crosses a heterozygous fly (Ww) with a vestigial-winged fly (ww). What is the probability that any one offspring of this cross will be heterozygous?
items.explain:
Set up the cross Ww × ww:

Ww
wWwww
wWwww

2 of the 4 boxes are Ww: 2 ÷ 4 = 50%.

25% is the chance of a ww offspring in the first cross (Ww × Ww), not this one.
why: 25% is the chance of a ww fly from the first cross (Ww × Ww). In Ww × ww, two of the four boxes are Ww: 50%.
75% is the share of normal-winged flies in a Ww × Ww cross. In this cross, only 2 of 4 boxes are Ww: 50%.
Not every offspring is Ww. The ww parent gives only w, and the Ww parent gives W half the time, so half the offspring are Ww and half are ww.

items.prompt: From the original Ww × Ww cross, the researcher raises 400 offspring. About how many of them would be expected to have normal wings?
items.explain:
Normal wings appear in WW and Ww flies: 3 of the 4 Punnett square boxes (WW, Ww, Ww), or 3/4 = 75%.

400 × 0.75 = 300 flies.

100 is the expected number of vestigial (ww) flies, and 200 counts only the heterozygous (Ww) flies, leaving out the WW flies, which also have normal wings.
why: 100 is the expected number of vestigial (ww) flies, 1/4 of 400. Normal wings include WW and Ww: 3/4 of 400 = 300.
200 counts only the heterozygous Ww flies. WW flies also have normal wings, so 3/4 of 400 = 300.
Not every fly has normal wings; 1 of 4 boxes is ww (vestigial). Expect 3/4 of 400 = 300 normal-winged flies.

items.prompt: Which statement describes the relationship shown in the data?
options: As the mass of the cart increases, its acceleration also increases.
The acceleration of the cart does not depend on its mass.
As the mass of the cart increases, the force on the cart decreases.
As the mass of the cart increases, its acceleration decreases.
items.explain:
With the same 12 N force, a 2 kg cart accelerated at 6.0 m/s2, while a 6 kg cart accelerated at only 2.0 m/s2. As mass increases, acceleration decreases (an inverse relationship: a = F/m).

The force did not change; it was 12 N in every trial. The data clearly show acceleration changing with mass, so it does depend on mass.
why: You reversed the trend. As mass rose from 2 kg to 6 kg, acceleration fell from 6.0 to 2.0 m/s<sup>2</sup>.
The acceleration clearly changed with mass, from 6.0 m/s<sup>2</sup> for 2 kg to 2.0 m/s<sup>2</sup> for 6 kg, so it does depend on mass.
The force was the same 12 N in every trial. What decreased as mass increased was the acceleration.

items.prompt: Using F = ma, how much force would be needed to give a 5 kg cart an acceleration of 4 m/s2?
options: 9 N
items.explain:
F = m × a
F = 5 kg × 4 m/s2 = 20 N

0.8 N comes from dividing 4 by 5, and 1.25 N from dividing 5 by 4; division is used only when solving for mass or acceleration. 9 N comes from adding instead of multiplying.
why: You divided 4 by 5. To find force, multiply mass by acceleration: F = 5 × 4 = 20 N.
You divided 5 by 4. Division is used only when solving for mass or acceleration; for force, F = ma = 5 × 4 = 20 N.
You added mass and acceleration (5 + 4). Newton's second law multiplies them: F = 5 × 4 = 20 N.

items.prompt: Which variable did the class keep the same in every trial so that the test would be fair?
options: The force pulling each cart
The mass of each cart
The acceleration of each cart
The color of each cart
items.explain:
The table shows 12 N of applied force in every trial, so force is the controlled (constant) variable.

Mass was deliberately changed (independent variable), and acceleration was measured (dependent variable). Color was never mentioned or measured and would not affect the motion, so it is not a variable the class needed to control.
why: Mass was changed on purpose (2, 3, 4, and 6 kg), so it is the independent variable, not a controlled one.
Acceleration is what the motion sensor measured, so it is the dependent variable. The table shows the force (12 N) was the same in every trial.
Color is never mentioned in the investigation and would not affect motion. The variable the class kept constant was the 12 N force.

items.prompt: Sort the pond organisms listed below by feeding level, based on what each one eats in the food web.
items.explain:
Producer: Algae make their own food by photosynthesis; nothing in the list feeds the algae.

Primary consumers: Zooplankton and snails eat algae (the producer).

Secondary consumers: Minnows eat zooplankton, and crayfish eat snails, so both eat primary consumers.

A common mistake is calling snails secondary consumers because they are animals with shells; what matters is what they eat, and snails eat algae.
items.why: The most common error is putting snails with the secondary consumers because they are animals. Feeding level depends on what an organism eats: snails eat algae, so they are primary consumers; minnows and crayfish eat primary consumers, so they are secondary consumers.

items.prompt: Suppose the algae in the pond capture 50,000 kilocalories (kcal) of energy. About how much of that energy would reach the minnows through the zooplankton?
options: 45,000 kcal
5,000 kcal
500 kcal
50 kcal
items.explain:
Energy passes through two transfers: algae → zooplankton → minnows. About 10% passes at each step.

Algae to zooplankton: 50,000 × 0.10 = 5,000 kcal
Zooplankton to minnows: 5,000 × 0.10 = 500 kcal

5,000 kcal is the energy that reaches the zooplankton, which stops one step short. 45,000 kcal is the energy lost at the first step, not the energy passed on.
why: 45,000 kcal is the energy lost at the first step (90%), not the energy passed on. Only 10% moves up each level: 50,000 → 5,000 → 500.
5,000 kcal is the energy that reaches the zooplankton, one step short. Take 10% again to reach the minnows: 500 kcal.
You took 10% three times. Algae → zooplankton → minnows is only two transfers: 50,000 × 0.10 × 0.10 = 500 kcal.

items.prompt: A disease kills most of the zooplankton in the pond. Which change is most likely to happen soon afterward?
options: The snail population decreases because snails eat zooplankton.
The crayfish population increases because crayfish eat zooplankton.
The heron population increases because herons eat zooplankton.
The algae population increases because fewer zooplankton are eating algae.
items.explain:
Zooplankton eat algae. With most zooplankton gone, fewer algae are eaten, so the algae population is likely to increase.

The other choices misread the food web: snails eat algae (not zooplankton), crayfish eat snails, and herons eat minnows and bass. None of those animals eat zooplankton directly.
why: The food web shows snails eat algae, not zooplankton. Losing zooplankton would not take away the snails' food.
Crayfish eat snails, not zooplankton. The organism most directly affected is the algae that zooplankton eat.
Herons eat minnows and bass, not zooplankton. If anything, fewer zooplankton means less food for minnows and then herons.

items.prompt: The student concluded that Trial 2 was the better test of the law of conservation of mass. Which reason best supports her conclusion?
options: The sealed bottle made the reaction produce more carbon dioxide than the open flask did.
Trial 2 started with a greater total mass of materials than Trial 1.
Every product of the reaction, including the gas, stayed inside the container that was weighed.
The cap kept the baking soda and vinegar from reacting, so nothing changed.
items.explain:
To test whether mass is conserved, every reactant and every product must be weighed before and after. The reaction makes carbon dioxide gas. In the open flask, the gas escaped into the room, so the balance missed it and the mass dropped by 245.0 − 242.6 = 2.4 g. In the sealed bottle, all of the products, including the gas, stayed in the container on the balance, so the mass stayed at 247.5 g, showing that matter was neither created nor destroyed.

The starting masses differ slightly, but the starting amount has nothing to do with whether the test is fair. Sealing the bottle does not make the reaction produce more gas, and the bubbling shows that the substances did react in Trial 2.
why: The cap does not make the reaction produce more gas. It only keeps the gas inside the container so its mass is counted.
A different starting mass does not make a test better. What matters is whether all products were weighed; in the open flask the CO<sub>2</sub> escaped.
The substances did react: the student tipped the bottle and bubbles formed. The cap kept the gas from escaping, so the mass stayed the same.

items.prompt:
Hydrogen gas reacts with oxygen gas to form water. Choose the coefficients that balance the equation.

{{0}} H2 + O2 → {{1}} H2O

why: With 1 H<sub>2</sub> there are only 2 hydrogen atoms, but 2 H<sub>2</sub>O needs 4. Use 2 H<sub>2</sub>.
3 H<sub>2</sub> gives 6 hydrogen atoms, but 2 H<sub>2</sub>O has only 4. Count atoms on both sides: 2 H<sub>2</sub>.
4 H<sub>2</sub> gives 8 hydrogen atoms, twice what 2 H<sub>2</sub>O contains. The balanced coefficient is 2.
1 H<sub>2</sub>O has only 1 oxygen atom, but O<sub>2</sub> supplies 2. You need 2 H<sub>2</sub>O.
3 H<sub>2</sub>O has 3 oxygen atoms, but O<sub>2</sub> supplies only 2. Use 2 H<sub>2</sub>O.
4 H<sub>2</sub>O has 4 oxygen atoms, but only one O<sub>2</sub> (2 atoms) is on the left. Use 2 H<sub>2</sub>O.

items.explain:
Start with oxygen: O2 has 2 oxygen atoms, so the product side needs 2 H2O (2 oxygen atoms).

Now 2 H2O contains 4 hydrogen atoms, so the reactant side needs 2 H2 (4 hydrogen atoms).

Check: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O has 4 H and 2 O on each side. Writing 1 H2 + O2 → 1 H2O leaves 2 O on the left but only 1 O on the right, so it is not balanced.

items.prompt: An atom of sodium has 11 protons, 12 neutrons, and 11 electrons. What is the mass number of this atom?
items.explain:
Mass number = protons + neutrons (the particles in the nucleus).

11 + 12 = 23

11 is the atomic number (protons only). 22 adds protons and electrons, but electrons have very little mass and are not counted in the mass number.
why: 11 is the atomic number, the number of protons only. Mass number adds the neutrons too: 11 + 12 = 23.
12 is the number of neutrons only. Mass number counts all particles in the nucleus: 11 protons + 12 neutrons = 23.
You added protons and electrons. Electrons have very little mass and are not counted; mass number = protons + neutrons = 23.

items.prompt: A student stirs 80 g of potassium nitrate into 100 g of water at 40 °C. About how much potassium nitrate will remain undissolved?
options: 0 g
items.explain:
At 40 °C, at most 64 g dissolves in 100 g of water.

80 g added − 64 g dissolved = 16 g undissolved.

48 g comes from using the 20 °C value (80 − 32), the wrong row. 64 g is the amount that dissolves, not the amount left over.
why: At 40 °C only 64 g can dissolve, and 80 g was added. The extra 80 − 64 = 16 g stays as solid.
You used the 20 °C row (80 − 32). The water is at 40 °C, where 64 g dissolves, leaving 16 g.
64 g is the amount that dissolves, not the amount left over. Subtract: 80 − 64 = 16 g undissolved.

items.prompt: Which statement is best supported by the data in the table?
options: Potassium nitrate dissolves equally well at all water temperatures.
The solubility of potassium nitrate rises by the same amount for every 20 °C increase.
Potassium nitrate does not dissolve at all at 0 °C.
The solubility of potassium nitrate increases as water temperature increases.
items.explain:
The maximum mass that dissolves rises at every step: 13 → 32 → 64 → 110 → 169 g. So solubility increases as temperature increases.

The increases are not equal (+19, +32, +46, +59 g), so the claim that solubility rises by the same amount every 20 °C is wrong. At 0 °C, 13 g still dissolves, so it does dissolve.
why: The table shows the amount rising from 13 g to 169 g as the water warms, so it does not dissolve equally at all temperatures.
The increases are not equal: +19, +32, +46, and +59 g. Solubility rises faster at higher temperatures.
The table shows 13 g dissolves at 0 °C, so it does dissolve, just not much.

items.prompt: How much kinetic energy, in joules, does the cart have at point B?
items.explain:
Total mechanical energy stays the same. At point A it is 9,800 J + 0 J = 9,800 J.

At point B: KE = total − PE = 9,800 − 4,900 = 4,900 J.

Check with point C: 7,350 + 2,450 = 9,800 J. A common error is answering 0 J by assuming kinetic energy appears only at the bottom; the cart is moving at every point below A.

mistakes.why: Kinetic energy is not only at the bottom; the cart is moving at every point below A. Total energy is 9,800 J, so KE at B = 9,800 − 4,900 = 4,900 J.
9,800 J is the total mechanical energy. At B, 4,900 J is still potential energy, so KE = 9,800 − 4,900 = 4,900 J.
You added PE at B to the total. Energy is conserved, so KE + PE = 9,800 J; KE = 9,800 − 4,900 = 4,900 J.

items.prompt: Classify each example by the main type of energy it shows. Drag each example into the correct category.
choices: A bowling ball rolling down a lane
Chemical energy stored in a battery
items.explain:
Kinetic energy is the energy of motion: the rolling bowling ball and the moving wind.

Potential energy is stored energy: the stretched rubber band (elastic), the water held high behind the dam (gravitational), and the battery (chemical energy stored in bonds).

A common mistake is calling the battery kinetic because it can power a moving device; until it is used, its energy is stored.
items.why: The most common error is putting the battery under kinetic energy because it can power something that moves. Until it is used, a battery's energy is stored in chemical bonds, so it is potential energy, like the stretched rubber band and the water behind the dam.

items.prompt: A metal spoon is left standing in a pot of hot soup. After a few minutes, the end of the handle sticking out of the pot feels hot. Which type of heat transfer mainly explains why the handle became hot?
options: Conduction
Convection
Radiation
Insulation
items.explain:
Conduction is the transfer of heat through direct contact, particle to particle, within a solid. Heat traveled from the soup into the spoon and along the metal to the handle.

Convection moves heat through the flow of liquids or gases; it helps circulate heat within the soup itself, but it does not move heat along a solid spoon. Insulation slows heat transfer rather than causing it.
why: Convection moves heat by the flow of a liquid or gas. It circulates heat within the soup, but heat travels along the solid metal spoon by direct contact: conduction.
Radiation transfers heat as waves through space, like heat from the Sun or a fire. The handle warmed because heat moved through the solid metal by contact: conduction.
Insulation slows heat transfer; it does not cause it. The spoon's metal carried heat to the handle by conduction.

items.prompt:
A simple circuit contains a battery and one light bulb. According to Ohm's law, V = IR (voltage = current × resistance), which changes would increase the current in the circuit?

Select two answers.
options: Using a battery with a higher voltage
Replacing the bulb with one that has a lower resistance
Replacing the bulb with one that has a higher resistance
Using a battery with a lower voltage
Adding a second bulb in series with the first
items.explain:
Rearrange Ohm's law to solve for current: I = V ÷ R.

Current increases when the voltage (top of the fraction) increases or when the resistance (bottom of the fraction) decreases. So a higher-voltage battery and a lower-resistance bulb both raise the current.

A higher-resistance bulb or a lower-voltage battery lowers the current. Adding a bulb in series adds resistance, which also lowers the current.
why: With I = V ÷ R, a larger resistance makes the current smaller, not larger.
With I = V ÷ R, a lower voltage makes the current smaller, not larger.
A second bulb in series adds resistance, and with I = V ÷ R, more resistance lowers the current.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains the change in the percent of resistant bacteria shown in the table?
options: Resistant bacteria survived each exposure and reproduced, so their share of the population grew.
The antibiotic caused each bacterium to develop resistance so that it could survive.
Resistant bacteria reproduce faster than other bacteria even when no antibiotic is present.
The researchers added more resistant bacteria to the population after each round.
items.explain:
This is natural selection. The passage says resistance comes from random mutations already present in a few cells. The antibiotic killed most nonresistant bacteria, while resistant bacteria survived and reproduced, so their percentage rose from 1% to 96%.

The antibiotic does not cause bacteria to develop resistance on purpose; it selects which existing bacteria survive. The passage gives no evidence about growth rates without an antibiotic or about researchers adding bacteria.
why: The passage says resistance comes from random mutations already present in a few cells. The antibiotic does not create resistance; it kills the others, so the resistant cells take over.
The passage gives no data on growth without the antibiotic. The rise happened because the antibiotic killed nonresistant cells while resistant ones survived and reproduced.
The passage says the researchers let the survivors regrow; they did not add bacteria. Natural selection explains the rise from 1% to 96%.

items.prompt:
Based on the passage, which actions would help slow the spread of antibiotic resistance?

Select two answers.
options: Taking the full course of an antibiotic as prescribed
Saving leftover antibiotics to use the next time you feel sick
Avoiding antibiotics for viral illnesses such as colds
Stopping an antibiotic as soon as symptoms improve
Sharing an antibiotic with a family member who has similar symptoms
items.explain:
The passage warns that stopping early and using antibiotics when they are not needed speed up resistance. So the helpful actions are the opposites: finishing the full course and not using antibiotics for viral illnesses, since antibiotics have no effect on viruses.

Stopping when symptoms improve leaves the hardest-to-kill bacteria alive. Saving or sharing leftover antibiotics leads to incomplete courses and unneeded use.
why: Saving leftovers means a course was not finished, and using them later may be for an illness that does not need them. The passage says both speed up resistance.
The passage warns that stopping early leaves the hardest-to-kill bacteria alive, which speeds up resistance.
Sharing gives each person an incomplete course and may treat an illness, such as a cold, that antibiotics cannot help. The passage says this speeds up resistance.

items.prompt: The release of insulin after a meal is an example of negative feedback. Which statement best explains why?
options: The response increases the original change, raising blood glucose even higher.
The response happens only in people who have type 1 diabetes.
The response reverses the original change, bringing blood glucose back toward normal.
The response stops the digestion of food in the stomach.
items.explain:
In negative feedback, the body's response works against the change that triggered it. Blood glucose rises after a meal; insulin causes cells to take in glucose, so the level falls back toward normal.

A response that increases the original change describes positive feedback. The passage says people with type 1 diabetes make little or no insulin, so the response is not limited to them; it is the normal process in a healthy body.
why: A response that increases the original change is positive feedback. Insulin lowers blood glucose after it rises, which reverses the change.
The passage says people with type 1 diabetes make little or no insulin. Insulin release is the normal process in a healthy body.
The passage says insulin signals cells to take in glucose; it says nothing about stopping digestion. Negative feedback means the response reverses the rise in glucose.

items.prompt: The sentences below describe parts of an animal cell. Click the sentence that describes the organelle where cellular respiration releases most of the energy the cell can use.
spans: The nucleus contains the cell's DNA and directs the cell's activities.
Ribosomes link amino acids together to build proteins.
Mitochondria use oxygen to finish breaking down glucose and produce ATP.
The cell membrane controls which substances enter and leave the cell.
Vacuoles store water, nutrients, and wastes.
items.explain:
Cellular respiration uses glucose and oxygen to make ATP, the cell's usable energy. Most of this ATP is made in the mitochondria.

The nucleus controls the cell but does not release energy from glucose. Ribosomes use energy to build proteins rather than produce it.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the nucleus sentence, because the nucleus “directs the cell's activities.” Directing is not releasing energy: the sentence about mitochondria using oxygen to break down glucose and produce ATP describes cellular respiration.

items.prompt: By what percent did the CO2 concentration increase from 1960 to 2020? Round to the nearest whole percent.
items.explain:
Percent change = (new − original) ÷ original × 100.

414 − 317 = 97 ppm
97 ÷ 317 ≈ 0.306
0.306 × 100 ≈ 30.6%, which rounds to 31%

A common error is dividing by the new value (97 ÷ 414 ≈ 23%). Always divide by the starting (original) value.

mistakes.why: You divided by the 2020 value (97 ÷ 414). Percent change divides by the starting value: 97 ÷ 317 ≈ 31%.
97 ppm is the amount of change, not the percent. Divide by the 1960 value: 97 ÷ 317 ≈ 0.306, or 31%.
131% is the 2020 value as a percent of the 1960 value. The increase is the part above 100%: 31%.

items.prompt: What was the average rate of increase in CO2 concentration from 2000 to 2020?
options: 1.1 ppm per year
1.6 ppm per year
2.2 ppm per year
4.4 ppm per year
items.explain:
Rate = change in concentration ÷ change in time.

414 − 370 = 44 ppm
2020 − 2000 = 20 years
44 ÷ 20 = 2.2 ppm per year

1.6 ppm per year is the average rate for the whole 1960–2020 period (97 ÷ 60 ≈ 1.6), not for 2000–2020. 1.1 comes from dividing 44 by 40 years instead of 20, and 4.4 comes from dividing by 10 years instead of 20.
why: You divided 44 ppm by 40 years. From 2000 to 2020 is 20 years: 44 ÷ 20 = 2.2.
1.6 ppm per year is the average rate for the whole period, 1960 to 2020 (97 ÷ 60). For 2000 to 2020, use 44 ÷ 20 = 2.2.
You divided 44 ppm by 10 years. The period from 2000 to 2020 is 20 years: 44 ÷ 20 = 2.2.

items.prompt: Along the western coast of South America, an oceanic plate is moving toward a continental plate and sinking beneath it. Based on the passage, which features would scientists most expect to find in this region?
options: A deep ocean trench offshore and a chain of volcanoes on land
An underwater ridge where new crust forms as the plates move apart
A long fault where the plates slide past each other with no volcanoes
A wide area where crust is neither created nor destroyed and earthquakes never occur
items.explain:
An oceanic plate sinking beneath a continental plate is subduction at a convergent boundary. The passage says subduction forms a deep ocean trench offshore and a chain of volcanoes on the continent.

An underwater ridge with new crust describes a divergent boundary, where plates move apart. Plates sliding past each other describes a transform boundary.
why: An underwater ridge with new crust describes a divergent boundary, where plates move apart. Here the plates move toward each other and one sinks: subduction.
Plates sliding past each other describe a transform boundary. Here one plate sinks under the other, which the passage says forms a trench and volcanoes.
The passage says crust is neither created nor destroyed only at transform boundaries, and those still have earthquakes. This region is a subduction zone.

items.prompt: Scientists collect rock samples from the floor of the Atlantic Ocean at increasing distances from the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Based on the passage, which result would they most likely find?
options: The rocks are younger the farther they are from the ridge.
The rocks are all about the same age.
The oldest rocks are found at the center of the ridge.
The rocks are older the farther they are from the ridge.
items.explain:
New crust forms at the ridge and is carried away on both sides as more new crust forms behind it. So the youngest rock is at the ridge, and rock gets older with distance from the ridge.

The reversed choices (younger farther away, oldest at the ridge) confuse where crust is created. The rocks cannot all be the same age, because crust is formed continuously over time.
why: You reversed the pattern. New crust forms at the ridge and is carried outward, so rock is youngest at the ridge and older farther away.
Crust forms continuously at the ridge and moves outward, so the rocks cannot all be the same age.
The ridge is where new crust is made, so the youngest rocks are at the center, not the oldest.

items.prompt: Which pattern is shown in the table?
options: Planets farther from the Sun take longer to complete one orbit.
Planets farther from the Sun always have thicker atmospheres.
Surface temperature decreases with every increase in distance from the Sun.
Planets closer to the Sun take longer to complete one orbit.
items.explain:
As distance increases (0.39 → 0.72 → 1.00 → 1.52 → 5.20 AU), orbital period increases at every step (0.24 → 0.62 → 1.00 → 1.88 → 11.86 years). So farther planets take longer to orbit.

Temperature does not drop at every step: Venus (464 °C) is hotter than Mercury (167 °C) even though it is farther away. Atmosphere thickness does not follow distance either: Mars is farther than Earth but has a thinner atmosphere.
why: Mars is farther from the Sun than Earth but has a thin atmosphere, so thickness does not follow distance.
Venus (464 °C) is hotter than Mercury (167 °C) even though it is farther away, so temperature does not drop at every step.
You reversed the pattern. Mercury, the closest, takes 0.24 years; Jupiter, the farthest, takes 11.86 years.

items.prompt: Venus is almost twice as far from the Sun as Mercury, yet its average surface temperature is much higher. Which explanation is best supported by the table?
options: Venus is closer to the Sun than Mercury is.
Venus's very thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat near its surface.
Venus takes longer to orbit the Sun, so it absorbs more sunlight each year.
Mercury's thick atmosphere reflects most of the sunlight that reaches it.
items.explain:
The table shows that Venus has a very thick atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide, while Mercury has almost none. Carbon dioxide traps heat (the greenhouse effect), so Venus stays hotter than Mercury.

The table shows Venus is farther from the Sun (0.72 AU vs. 0.39 AU), not closer. Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so it cannot have a thick, reflective one. A longer orbital period does not mean more sunlight is absorbed; Venus receives less sunlight than Mercury because it is farther away.
why: The table shows Venus at 0.72 AU and Mercury at 0.39 AU, so Venus is farther away, not closer.
A longer orbit does not mean more sunlight absorbed. Venus is farther away, so it receives less sunlight; its thick CO<sub>2</sub> atmosphere is what traps heat.
The table says Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so it cannot have a thick, reflective one.
